Cue.Title: The spectacle only works because the rules underneath are real.
Cue.Description: Next: why PC buying is a constraint problem—and how the compatibility resolver keeps domain logic independent from the 3D scene.

Intro.Title: A beautiful build is still wrong if the parts disagree.
Intro.Description: PC configuration is a chain of physical, electrical, and platform constraints. BASE 60 makes those rules visible before a customer commits to a build.

Model.Label: Resolver contract
Model.Description: The compatibility layer receives a component manifest and returns structured findings. The 3D scene consumes that result; it does not own the rules.
Model.Note: A pure resolver keeps domain decisions testable, reusable, and independent from presentation timing.

Question.Label: The buyer's question
Question.Title: Will these parts actually work together?
Question.Description: The interface answers with a reason, not a mysterious disabled button: socket mismatch, memory generation conflict, insufficient power, or a clearance limit.

Rules.Title: Six families carry the engineering risk.
Rules.Description: Each family maps to a decision the resolver can explain. The list is intentionally concrete: it gives the visual builder an operational vocabulary.

Socket.Title: Socket + chipset
Socket.Description: Match CPU and motherboard sockets, then account for chipset and BIOS support.

Memory.Title: Memory generation
Memory.Description: Keep DDR generation, capacity, and board limits aligned with the selected platform.

Power.Title: Power + connectors
Power.Description: Compare system demand with PSU capacity and the connectors the build requires.

Clearance.Title: GPU clearance
Clearance.Description: Check card length against chassis clearance before a physical fit becomes a return.

Thermal.Title: Cooling envelope
Thermal.Description: Validate cooler height, radiator dimensions, and the case's thermal headroom.

Storage.Title: M.2 + expansion
Storage.Description: Respect M.2 slots, lane sharing, and the expansion layout of the chosen board.

Flow.Title: One source of truth, four ways to experience it.
Flow.Description: The same result can guide a product card, a builder alert, a cart guard, or an admin review because the rule engine is not coupled to one screen.

Input.Title: Manifest
Input.Description: Selected parts and their compatibility metadata enter as structured input.

Resolver.Title: Rules
Resolver.Description: Pure checks compare sockets, dimensions, power, thermals, and expansion.

State.Title: Shared state
State.Description: Zustand carries the build and structured alerts across the experience.

Scene.Title: 3D feedback
Scene.Description: The Crucible renders the current assembly and makes conflicts legible.

Flow.Boundary: The visual layer can animate, explain, and recover from a conflict without silently rewriting the domain decision.

Prologue.Title: Can chaos break an image—and put every pixel back?
Prologue.Proposition: A graduation research project combining nonlinear dynamics, a dynamic RGB S-box, and a desktop application to investigate reversible color-image encryption.
Prologue.ResearchBoundary: This is an academic proof of concept. The reported experiments are presented as research evidence, not as an independently audited or production-ready cryptographic claim.

Cue.Title: The interface is only the instrument. The case starts with the transformation pipeline.
Cue.Description: Next: how five coupled nonlinear equations become a dynamic RGB substitution box, then a reversible pixel transformation.

Intro.Title: The key material begins as motion, not a stored pattern.
Intro.Description: Five coupled nonlinear state variables evolve from the supplied initial conditions. Their trajectories feed an RGB substitution box, which becomes the repeatable key field used by the image transform.
Intro.Boundary: This chapter documents the implemented research method. It explains reversibility and engineering choices; it does not claim that those properties establish modern cryptographic security.

System.Title: Five equations generate the changing state.
System.Description: The system couples x, y, z, u, and v through linear, multiplicative, and sinusoidal terms. Small changes to the starting state produce a different numerical trajectory for the experiment.
System.Note: The displayed equations and solver settings are transcribed from the working Python implementation.

Pipeline.Title: One numerical trajectory becomes a reversible image pipeline.
Pipeline.Description: Each stage has a specific job: establish the state, sample it, map it into RGB values, transform the image, then perform the inverse in the opposite order.

Seed.Title: Seed five states
Seed.Description: The user supplies initial values for x, y, z, u, and v together with an S-box size.

Solve.Title: Integrate the system
Solve.Description: SciPy numerically solves the coupled equations and returns five evolving sequences.

SBox.Title: Map three RGB streams
SBox.Description: Derived x, y, and z sequences are reduced to 8-bit channel values and arranged as a color S-box.

Transform.Title: Tile, XOR, shift
Transform.Description: The S-box repeats across the image. Each channel is XORed with its key field, then shifted modulo 256.

Reverse.Title: Undo in reverse
Reverse.Description: Decryption subtracts the value shift first, then applies the same XOR key field to recover the pixels.

Reversal.Title: The order is what makes the transform reversible.
Reversal.Description: P is the source-channel value, K is the corresponding tiled S-box value, s is the configured shift, and C is the encrypted value.
Reversal.Note: The implementation performs a modular pixel-value shift. It does not spatially rotate or rearrange pixel positions.

Vector.Title: Operate on image planes, not one pixel at a time.
Vector.Description: The first approach expressed the algorithm as nested channel, row, and column loops. The working path tiles the S-box with NumPy and transforms complete channel arrays, reducing Python-level work while preserving the same inverse operation.

Next.Title: A reversible pipeline is only the beginning. The next chapter examines what the experiments actually measured.

Intro.Title: A number matters only when its claim stays in bounds.
Intro.Description: The research evaluated statistical behavior, sensitivity, visual similarity, recovery, and execution time. This chapter keeps the reported results visible alongside the limits of their interpretation.
Intro.Boundary: These values come from the supplied graduation paper and its representative 256 × 256 image experiments. They have not been independently reproduced or security-audited for this portfolio.

Metrics.Title: Eight signals describe the experiment from different angles.
Metrics.Description: No single score validates an encryption design. Read together, the measurements describe the output distribution, response to change, recovery fidelity, and observed runtime.
Metrics.SourceNote: Values are reported to their paper precision. Precision in the table does not imply independent verification or broader generalization.

Entropy.Label: Encrypted entropy
Entropy.Note: Reported information density near the 8-bit upper bound.

NPCR.Label: NPCR
NPCR.Note: Reported percentage of changed encrypted pixels under the paper's comparison.

UACI.Label: UACI
UACI.Note: Reported average intensity change between compared cipher images.

Horizontal.Label: Horizontal correlation
Horizontal.Note: Reported adjacent-pixel coefficient in the encrypted image.

Vertical.Label: Vertical correlation
Vertical.Note: Reported adjacent-pixel coefficient in the encrypted image.

PSNR.Label: Original → encrypted PSNR
PSNR.Note: Low reported similarity between the source and encrypted image.

SSIM.Label: Recovery fidelity
SSIM.Note: Original-to-decrypted structural similarity reported as exact recovery.

Time.Label: Encryption time
Time.Note: Typical reported runtime for the paper's representative experiment.

Reading.Title: Separate what the test supports from what it cannot certify.
Reading.Description: The useful story is not that every value is high or low. It is that each metric answers a narrower question about the experiment.

Randomness.Title: Distribution
Randomness.Supports: Entropy near 8 bits, near-zero adjacent correlation, and low original-to-encrypted PSNR are consistent with a visually flattened output unlike its source.
Randomness.Limit: Statistical appearance alone does not establish resistance to cryptanalysis, key recovery, or structural attacks.

Sensitivity.Title: Change sensitivity
Sensitivity.Supports: The reported NPCR and UACI values indicate that the tested comparison produced broad pixel and intensity changes.
Sensitivity.Limit: A representative differential test is not a substitute for a defined threat model or systematic adversarial evaluation.

Recovery.Title: Reversibility
Recovery.Supports: An original-to-decrypted SSIM of 1.0 supports lossless recovery for the reported test image and parameters.
Recovery.Limit: Successful inversion confirms implementation behavior, not confidentiality or authenticity under attack.

Runtime.Title: Observed speed
Runtime.Supports: The reported 0.7–0.8 second encryption time shows the vectorized prototype was interactive in its test setting.
Runtime.Limit: It is not a cross-device benchmark, scale guarantee, or real-time performance claim.

Artifact.Title: The interface keeps the experiment inspectable.
Artifact.Description: Original, encrypted, generated S-box, and decrypted states appear together, allowing the researcher to run and visually review the complete transformation loop.
Artifact.Label: Image cryptography research artifact
Artifact.Caption: The working desktop application presents the source image, encrypted result, generated RGB S-box, and recovered image in one research workspace.
Artifact.Proves: This artifact demonstrates a working end-to-end desktop experiment; it does not independently validate cryptographic security.

Limits.Title: Credibility grows when the unknowns remain visible.

Dataset.Title: Representative scope
Dataset.Description: The supplied results describe representative 256 × 256 color-image experiments, not a broad standardized corpus.

Reproduction.Title: Reported, not rerun
Reproduction.Description: This portfolio records the paper's measurements. It does not present a fresh independent benchmark run or reproducibility package.

Audit.Title: No independent audit
Audit.Description: The system remains an academic proof of concept and should not be treated as suitable for security-critical production use.

Next.Title: The final layer is the product work: turning a mathematical experiment into a usable desktop research instrument.

Intro.Title: The research became something another person could operate.
Intro.Description: The desktop application connects configuration, transformation, visual inspection, measurement, and export in one controlled workflow. The interface is not decoration around the algorithm; it is how the experiment becomes repeatable and understandable.
Intro.Boundary: This chapter documents implemented desktop behavior visible in the supplied source and application artifact. It does not claim commercial adoption, accessibility certification, or production-security readiness.

Workspace.Title: Keep the full transformation loop in view.
Workspace.Description: The main workspace places source, cipher, generated S-box, and recovered image side by side. Inputs and actions stay beneath the evidence, while a separate Evaluation tab handles measurement and plotting.
Workspace.Caption: Interface reconstruction based on the working application structure; it explains information architecture rather than replacing the real screenshot above.

Workflow.Title: Configure, run, inspect, preserve.
Workflow.Description: The product follows the sequence of an experiment instead of exposing implementation modules as disconnected controls.

Configure.Title: Configure the experiment
Configure.Description: Load an image, normalize it to RGB when needed, enter five initial conditions, and choose an S-box size.

Run.Title: Run the transformation
Run.Description: Encrypt and decrypt on worker threads while progress feedback keeps the desktop interface responsive.

Inspect.Title: Inspect the evidence
Inspect.Description: Compare four image states, update metrics, view three histograms, and plot chaotic-system trajectories.

Export.Title: Preserve or repeat
Export.Description: Save encrypted, decrypted, and S-box PNG files—or reload an encrypted image with matching parameters for decryption.

Capabilities.Title: A small application covers the complete research cycle.

Items.RGB: Load PNG, JPG, or JPEG and convert non-RGB input.
Items.Conditions: Edit all five chaotic-system initial conditions.
Items.SBoxSize: Choose and validate the substitution-box size.

Items.Previews: Review original, encrypted, S-box, and decrypted states together.
Items.Metrics: Calculate statistical, similarity, correlation, and timing metrics.
Items.Plots: Open image histograms and chaotic trajectory plots.

Items.Async: Run encryption and decryption outside the UI thread.
Items.Reload: Load an encrypted image into a dedicated decryption path.
Items.Themes: Switch between ttkbootstrap light and dark themes.

Items.PNG: Export encrypted, decrypted, and generated S-box images.
Items.Executable: Package the application as a standalone Windows executable.
Items.Resources: Resolve bundled assets consistently in development and PyInstaller builds.

Stack.Title: The mathematics stays separated from the interface that operates it.
Stack.Description: A modular structure lets the GUI coordinate work without owning the chaotic model, transformation logic, or evaluation formulas.

Interface.Title: Tkinter + ttkbootstrap
Interface.Description: Tabs, inputs, previews, progress, dialogs, and theme switching.

Orchestrator.Title: ImageEncryptor
Orchestrator.Description: Image state, S-box generation, forward and inverse transforms, and export methods.

Numerical.Title: NumPy + SciPy
Numerical.Description: Vectorized channel operations and numerical integration of the five-dimensional system.

Analysis.Title: Pillow + scikit-image + Matplotlib
Analysis.Description: Image I/O, similarity and statistical evaluation, histograms, and trajectory plots.

Package.Title: PyInstaller
Package.Description: Windows executable packaging with runtime-safe paths for bundled resources.

Decisions.Title: Three choices turned a script into an instrument.

Workspace.Title: Show the loop, not isolated outputs.
Workspace.Description: Keeping all four image states visible makes reversibility inspectable and reduces the mental work of comparing separate files or windows.

Threading.Title: Keep numerical work off the UI thread.
Threading.Description: Encryption and decryption run in worker threads; UI updates return through Tkinter's event loop so progress remains visible during computation.

Validation.Title: Reject invalid experiments early.
Validation.Description: The interface checks missing images, numeric initial conditions, positive S-box size, and image-size bounds before starting the transformation.

Package.Title: From Python project to a Windows application.
Package.Description: A PyInstaller specification, application icon, and runtime resource-path helper package the research workspace so it can run outside the development environment.

Next.Title: The closing chapter will connect the research contribution, engineering ownership, and the work required before any security-critical use.

Outcome.Title: A mathematical proposal became a complete, inspectable software experiment.

Intro.Title: The product promise depends on boundaries people can trust.

Decisions.Title: Make the safe path the understandable path.

Organization.Title: Derive tenant context from verified organization membership.
Organization.Context: Loose lab identifiers make it too easy for a request boundary to drift away from the signed-in organization.
Organization.Choice: Use Better Auth Organizations as the canonical membership layer and link the Lab domain entity to it.
Organization.Tradeoff: Every server action must carry and validate context deliberately while legacy paths are migrated.
Organization.Evidence: The brief documents this as the current tenancy migration focus; production isolation results are not claimed here.

Permissions.Title: Centralize permissions instead of scattering role checks.
Permissions.Context: As a product grows, ad-hoc role conditions become hard to audit and can disagree across actions.
Permissions.Choice: Use version-controlled role bundles, explicit permissions, centralized evaluation, and default-deny behavior.
Permissions.Tradeoff: The policy surface needs design, tests, and migration effort before every module can rely on it.
Permissions.Evidence: The current brief names Owner, Admin, Manager, and Staff rules plus resource policies; it does not claim complete rollout.

Staff.Title: Keep a person’s job record separate from their application access.
Staff.Context: A laboratory may need to track a technician who does not have a LabOS account—or revoke access without deleting the staff record.
Staff.Choice: Model staff records and application members separately, then link them through explicit invitation and membership flows.
Staff.Tradeoff: Lifecycle operations become more deliberate, but access changes no longer erase domain history or rely on implied roles.
Staff.Evidence: This separation is a stated product and architecture rule in the supplied LabOS brief.

Decisions.Title: Three choices shaped the product more than any visual detail.

Desktop.Title: Build for the computers already in the laboratory.
Desktop.Context: The product needed to fit a Windows-based working environment and support a dense operational interface.
Desktop.Choice: Use C# and WPF on .NET for a native desktop application with direct OS integration.
Desktop.Tradeoff: The result is intentionally Windows-specific and requires desktop packaging and update management.
Desktop.Evidence: Supported by Oscar’s published platform and technology inventory; device distribution is not publicly documented.

Data.Title: Keep the operational record local and recoverable.
Data.Context: A laboratory needed day-to-day control of its records without making a hosted service part of every operation.
Data.Choice: Use SQLite through Entity Framework Core, with import, export, backup, and restore paths.
Data.Tradeoff: Backup discipline becomes explicit, and this case study does not claim multi-device synchronization.
Data.Evidence: Supported by the documented SQLite, EF Core, database import, export, backup, and restore capabilities.

Delivery.Title: Treat licensing and updates as part of the product.
Delivery.Context: Commercial desktop software needs controlled activation and a practical way to deliver fixes after installation.
Delivery.Choice: Use a GitHub-backed activation process and AutoUpdater.NET for release checks and installer delivery.
Delivery.Tradeoff: Activation and updates depend on external connectivity and GitHub availability, while operational data remains local.
Delivery.Evidence: Supported by the documented activation flow, Octokit/GitHub API integration, and AutoUpdater.NET technology inventory.
